title: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
description: From Mechanistic Insights to Future Translation and Innovation

blocks.text: Companies news

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: From Mechanistic Insights to Future Translation and Innovation

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: Purpose and focus

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: How should we live and work to reduce the burden on the planet?

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: Rethinking healthy life expectancy and working life as tools for environmental sustainability

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: Today, we face serious global challenges, including climate change, biodiversity loss, and shortages of natural resources. These problems are not only about energy or technology. They are also closely linked to how people live and how people work.

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: At the same time, advances in medicine, nutrition, and living conditions mean that people can live longer and stay healthier for more years than before. Until now, longer healthy lives and longer working lives have mainly been discussed in terms of personal well-being, social security, or labor shortages.

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: In this symposium, we take a different perspective.

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: We ask a simple but important question:Can longer healthy lives and working lives be used as tools to reduce the burden on the planet?

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: When illness and long-term care are concentrated in the later stages of life, society needs large amounts of medical services, care workers, materials, and energy. This places a heavy burden not only on society but also on the environment. If more people can stay healthy for longer, it may be possible to reduce these pressures and change how resources are used across society.

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: Working longer does not have to mean producing more and consuming more. It can also mean sharing knowledge, supporting others, caring for communities, and protecting nature. These are forms of work that contribute to society while using fewer resources.

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: This symposium explores practical ways to extend healthy life expectancy and working life while reducing environmental impact, focusing on the following themes:

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: Food: Diets that are good for both human health and the planet

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: Physical activity: Everyday movement to maintain health and prevent disease

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: Sleep: Improving sleep quality to support mental and physical well-being

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: Disease prevention: Preventing illness rather than treating it after it occurs

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: Gut microbiota: Living in balance with the microorganisms in our bodies

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: Stem cell biology: Science that supports functional health, not life extension at any cost

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: All of these approaches have the potential not only to improve individual health but also to reduce the demand for medical and care services and ultimately to lower the environmental burden.

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: This symposium brings together researchers, companies, policymakers, and people from many different backgrounds to think together about one key question:

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: What does a society look like where people can live long, healthy lives that are also kind to the planet?

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: By rethinking longer, healthier lives and working lives not only for individuals but also as a choice for the planet and future generations, this symposium aims to open new paths toward a more sustainable future.

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: REGISTER

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: For companies

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: This symposium explores a new idea: can longer, healthier lives help reduce environmental impact?

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: As climate change and resource limits become major business risks, companies are being asked to rethink not only energy and materials, but also how people live and work. Advances in health and life sciences now allow people to stay healthy and active for much longer. This symposium views healthy life expectancy and working life not as goals in themselves, but as tools for environmental sustainability.

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: By reducing the need for resource-intensive medical and care services, and by promoting low-impact forms of work such as knowledge sharing and community support, long healthy lives can become part of an environmental strategy.

blocks.section: International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026
blocks.text: Participation offers companies a chance to connect environmental, health, and human capital strategies in a single, forward-looking dialogue. If you can attend and support our activities, we would greatly appreciate it. title: Interview with Jean-Marc Peillex: a collaboration between Saint-Gervais and Yamanouchi
description:
Jean-Marc Peillex, Mayor of Saint-Gervais, was in Japan to strengthen a strategic partnership between his town and Yamanouchi. In this interview, he looks back at this collaboration’s origins, aims and prospects.

▶️ 11 minutes ? Language : french - available subtitles : french and english 


The birth of the partnership: The partnership between Saint-Gervais and Yamanouchi was born out of opportunities and meetings facilitated by the Lyon consulate. The two towns, which share similarities in profile (ski resorts, thermal baths and mountains), quickly agreed to formalise the agreement. A protocol was signed to develop joint projects in less than a year.
Objectives and initiatives: Jean-Marc Peillex explains that this partnership goes well beyond traditional twinning. The aim is to create cultural and educational exchanges between young people. Initiatives involving schools and municipal children's councils are underway, with planned exchanges. Another crucial area is gastronomy. The two towns want to organise culinary exchanges to promote their local specialities.
Knowledge transfer: Saint-Gervais is contributing its expertise in ski resort management and sustainable development. Jean-Marc Peillex emphasises the importance of limiting excessive infrastructure, consolidating ski lifts and diversifying activities beyond winter to exploit the potential of all four seasons.
Enhancing the value of the area: The mayor stresses the importance of developing a policy centred on the local population. In Saint-Gervais, this approach has helped to stem the rural exodus and increase the permanent population. He encourages Yamanouchi to adopt a similar approach to preserve local life and avoid exclusive dependence on seasonal tourism.
Climate change and snow cover: Although the French Alps are facing increasing challenges from global warming, Yamanouchi still benefits from abundant natural snow cover. Jean-Marc Peillex stresses the importance for Japan of exploiting this opportunity to attract visitors while remaining respectful of the environment.
A model for the future: Saint-Gervais is presented as an example of a balanced resort, active 11 months out of 12, thanks to a policy that intelligently mixes permanent residents, tourists and diversified activities. The mayor hopes that this model can inspire Yamanouchi.
Conclusion: This collaboration is a unique opportunity for two mountain regions, united by their ambition to develop sustainable tourism, to share experiences and create value.

title: Interview with Loïg Chesnais-Girard, President of the Regional Council of Brittany
description:
Discover our exclusive interview with Loïg Chesnais-Girard, President of the Regional Council of Brittany, during his visit to Japan.
Through cultural anecdotes and strong economic ties, he reflects on the unique bond between Brittany and Japan. He shares his vision on key sectors such as agribusiness, space, telecommunications, and the future of health and innovation. An insightful interview highlighting the region's rising influence and the essential role of Japanese investors. A must-watch!
 A MUST-WATCH!*
*English subtitles available

Detailed summary of the interview with Mr. Girard, President of the Brittany Region:
Introduction: The interview begins with a warm welcome to Mr. Girard, who discusses the historical importance of Brittany in the economic relationship between France and Japan. Although Brittany is not located in central France, it has played a key role in initial Japanese investments in France, particularly in the 1980s when companies like Canon set up their operations.
A special connection between Japan and Brittany: Mr. Girard explains that this connection has deep historical roots. Brittany has always been open to the world, notably through maritime trade. Its ancestors were probably among the first to engage with other cultures and people, establishing historical ties with nations like Japan. He also highlights the shared values between the two regions, such as work ethic, commitment, and respect for promises, which are strong in both Brittany and Japan. A significant example for him is the commitment of Canon's employees in Brittany, which played a pivotal role in the company's decision not to close its factory in the region. Mr. Girard also emphasises the similarities in landscapes between Brittany and Japan, notably their strong connection to the sea and horizon and the importance of regional identity, which is experienced with pride in both cultures.
Personal memories and the arrival of Japanese companies: Mr Girard recalls the arrival of Japanese companies in the 1980s, a time marked by scepticism and fears about the presence of foreign companies, sometimes called "screwdriver factories." Many doubted their true intentions, such as concerns that they might be here solely for tax advantages or to sell their products more effectively. However, trust was established over time, especially given Japan's comparable standard of living to Europe, which helped dispel the fears associated with emerging markets.
Japanese tourism in Brittany: Regarding Japanese tourism, Mr. Girard explains that it remains small but steady, with around 15,000 Japanese visitors coming to Brittany each year. However, most Japanese tourists still prefer other regions in France, such as Paris, Bordeaux, or Mont-Saint-Michel. Although an attractive destination, Brittany has yet to become a must-visit place for Japanese tourists. Mr. Girard stresses the importance of making it easier for Japanese tourists to visit Brittany, encouraging them to cross the Couesnon River to explore places like Cancale, Saint-Malo, and Dinard.
Cuisine and seafood products: Gastronomy, particularly seafood, is another area of convergence between Brittany and Japan. Mr. Girard mentions seaweed, shellfish, and other specific products from Brittany found in Japan. He sees potential for collaboration in exploring these flavours and creating exchanges centred on these culinary products, focusing on adding value to Breton exports.
Economic development and the future of Brittany: In discussing Brittany's economic future, Mr. Girard emphasises the importance of supporting workers in Breton factories owned by Japanese companies while focusing on emerging and innovative sectors. He highlights industries such as hydrogen, space, health, and cybersecurity, where Brittany has many promising companies. He notes that Brittany has a long industrial tradition and continues to invest in strategic sectors.
Japanese investors vs. other international investors: When asked to compare Japanese investors to those from other countries, such as the United States or China, Mr. Girard explains that Japanese investors tend to focus on long-term investments. They think beyond immediate goals, considering plans for 20, 30, or even 50 years. This approach aligns well with Brittany's focus on "long-term" strategies in its investments and economic plan.
The growing role of regions in France: Finally, Mr. Girard discusses the increasing role of French regions in economic and political matters. Although French regions still represent a small portion of public spending (2-3%), he points out that regional presidents, including himself, have taken on greater economic responsibilities. He emphasises the importance of this local proximity to businesses and local stakeholders, mainly when dealing with international investments. The ability of local elected officials to switch between international and regional levels is key to quickly responding to business needs and facilitating contacts between global economic players.
Conclusion: Mr. Girard concludes by stressing the importance of this combined local and international approach, which he believes will be crucial in addressing future economic challenges. He remains confident in Brittany's future and its role within Europe, while also recognising the evolving role of regions in France's political and economic landscape.

blocks.section: Invitation to join as signers of the Business Leaders’ Declaration for a Society with Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI)
blocks.text: A society where diversity, equity and inclusion are present is one where all of us can pursue our happiness, where we welcome different opinions and thoughts, where we exclude no one, and where we are more flexible and resilient.

blocks.section: Invitation to join as signers of the Business Leaders’ Declaration for a Society with Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI)
blocks.text: Such a society is essential for business growth, value creation and reduction of social divisions and disparities.

blocks.section: Invitation to join as signers of the Business Leaders’ Declaration for a Society with Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI)
blocks.text: It is important for all businesses to cultivate a culture where diverse talents flourish regardless of their gender identity, sexual orientation, ethnicity, age and disability. It is imperative to provide the same opportunities and benefits to all partners, regardless of marital relation or gender identity, and to improve facilities and systems so they are user-friendly to all.

blocks.section: Invitation to join as signers of the Business Leaders’ Declaration for a Society with Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI)
blocks.text: We, the Business Leaders in Japan - host of the G7 - will take the lead in implementing these organizational changes and societal deployments in collaboration with key stakeholders, including the G7 national Chambers of Commerce and their related business communities, over the next four years to simultaneously realize "Society with DEI” and "Dynamic Economic Growth”.

title: Itinéraires singuliers Podcast- From Formula 1 to the political arena: Sakon Yamamoto's unique journey between Japan and the world
description:
From the absolute summit of motorsport to the Japanese national political stage, Sakon Yamamoto’s path illustrates a rare trajectory, shaped by competition, international experience, and a strong sense of commitment. A trajectory whose origins can be traced back to a decision made at the age of ten.In this episode of the Itinéraires Singuliers podcast, we welcome the former Formula 1 driver and former member of the House of Representatives to reflect on a journey where speed, risk, and responsibility constantly intersect.
Born in Toyohashi, in Aichi Prefecture, Sakon Yamamoto was introduced to motorsport at a very young age. At ten, reading a magazine article proved to be a turning point: he learned that starting racing after the age of twelve reduces the chances of reaching Formula 1 to less than 0.1 percent. For the child he was at the time, the conclusion was clear—time was running out. Without hesitation, he applied on his own initiative to the Suzuka Circuit Racing School.
The decision was not met with enthusiasm by his family. Motorsport is risky, uncertain, and expensive. Yet Yamamoto persisted—explaining, arguing, and insisting. Eventually, a compromise was reached: he would be allowed to try, under strict conditions. This marked the beginning of a demanding path, shaped early on by discipline and determination.
At the time, his role model was Ayrton Senna. The Brazilian driver embodied absolute excellence in his eyes. Senna’s sudden death in 1994 came as a shock, but it also triggered a profound shift in how Yamamoto viewed his own journey. No longer was the goal to resemble someone else, but rather to confront himself. Shortly thereafter, a sentence written on a New Year’s card from a senior driver left a lasting impression:
“We never imagine a dream that we are unable to achieve.”
This maxim would accompany him throughout his career.
In 2006, Sakon Yamamoto reached Formula 1. Among his most vivid memories is the Japanese Grand Prix at Suzuka. Racing with the Super Aguri F1 Team—an entirely Japanese outfit—he encountered a densely packed crowd at every corner of the circuit and an atmosphere unlike any other. That same season, at the Brazilian Grand Prix, the final round of the championship, he delivered a standout performance despite driving a technically outdated car. For the team, the result meant far more than a position in the standings: it symbolized cohesion and perseverance.
Often perceived as an individual sport, Formula 1 in fact relies on collective work of extreme precision. Engineers, mechanics, strategists, and driver must operate as a single unit. In a multicultural environment, Yamamoto learned the importance of dialogue, even in moments of tension. Mistakes are not failures in themselves; they become sources of learning. This approach, forged on the circuits, would extend well beyond the world of sport.
His years abroad also strengthened his awareness of Japanese identity. In Europe, he observed changes in the industrial and economic landscape: Japanese brands once omnipresent were gradually disappearing from public view. This observation generated both frustration and conviction—the belief that Japan still possesses considerable potential, provided the right conditions are created for it to be expressed.
It was in this context that the idea of political engagement emerged. For Yamamoto, this was not a radical break, but a continuation: after representing Japan on international circuits, why not contribute to its future in another way? Elected to the House of Representatives, he drew on his international experience, particularly in diplomacy, negotiation, and innovation‑related policy. He became especially involved in complex issues such as synthetic fuels, convinced that the energy transition could build on Japan’s industrial strengths.
Here again, the method remained the same: explain, persuade, bring people together—without giving up in the face of initial misunderstanding. The perseverance developed in Formula 1 found new resonance in the political arena.
Today, Sakon Yamamoto pursues an objective that is simple in its wording yet ambitious in its scope: to build a society in which everyone can say, “I am happy to have been born in Japan.” Disaster prevention, risk reduction, healthcare, and social protection lie at the heart of his concerns, with constant attention given to future generations.
This episode is not just the story of a sporting career. It demonstrates how experience gained at the highest level of competition can be extended into public service, and how one can move from international circuits to political responsibility without abandoning fundamental convictions.If you are interested in paths where sport, diplomacy, and innovation intersect—where engagement grows out of experience, and where an unconventional background sheds light on contemporary challenges facing Japan—we invite you to listen to this episode. It offers insight into how Sakon Yamamoto has put his international career at the service of public action, and what this transition reveals about the possible bridges between performance, responsibility, and politics today.

title: Itinéraires singuliers podcast - From the trading floor to sake breweries: Sébastien Lemoine’s rediscovered sense of purpose
description:
Leaving a well-established career in international finance to turn to Japanese sake may seem like a radical shift. For Sébastien Lemoine, it is above all the culmination of a quest: finding meaning again. That is the word he chooses to sum up his journey. After years on trading floors, in a demanding environment sometimes dominated by greed and performance, he realizes his energy is gradually fading. The shock of the global financial crisis, followed by the Tohoku disaster in 2011, accelerates his reflection.
Japan is a country he has known for a long time. He first came in 1986 as a student, drawn by the language and the culture. He then returned regularly, eventually settling there for extended periods. He has seen the country evolve, age, and change pace. What was once a very young, vibrant Japan - onsen full of children, overflowing energy in Roppongi - has given way to an older society. Yet his attachment has only grown stronger. He walks, cycles, crosses countryside and cities, and finds in this close relationship with the country a form of obviousness, almost a feeling of being “where he belongs”.
It was from 2008 that he truly discovered Japanese sake. Not generic sake, but carefully crafted bottles rooted in a culture of long-term commitment. Japanese craftsmanship, he says, is not just a profession but a path. One strives for a perfection that is never fully reached, but approached by integrating each year’s experience, variations in climate, rice, and microorganisms. He cites the Kenbishi brewery in Kobe, which claims continuity across centuries and blends each year sakes drawn from a fifty-year stock to maintain a consistent taste profile despite natural changes.
In a context where sake consumption has fallen by fourfold in fifty years and many breweries struggle to find successors, Sébastien chooses a different role: neither producer nor trader, but a transmitter. He creates Passerelle, a company whose name reflects its mission: building a bridge between Japanese producers and international audiences. He teaches at Le Cordon Bleu and Temple University, guides enthusiasts, and introduces this world through education and tasting.
The welcome he receives in sake breweries surprises him. He expected more reserve. Instead, he encounters artisans proud of their heritage yet deeply humble, often facing economic difficulties. He recalls a visit in Chiba where a producer, to mark their exchange, opened for him and a friend a bottle from 1952, her year of birth. This generosity, he often finds, emerges when he shows genuine interest and a serious understanding of the product.
Nothing was instantaneous, however. In Japan, legitimacy comes through expertise. Moving from a field where one is an expert to another where one is not yet requires learning, understanding processes, categories, and practices. This in-depth work, combined with recommendations and the trust of certain producers, gradually opens the doors of the industry to him.
His contribution also lies in an external perspective. Where sake breweries often present their product from a technical angle - water, rice, know-how - he emphasizes the tasting experience and food pairings. Drawing on his French culture of food and wine pairing, he proposes new approaches: sake with Western cuisine, sake with cheese, sake served not merely as an accompaniment but as an element that directly interacts with the dish. He sees this as a way to renew interest in a declining market.
He finally recalls the cultural and symbolic dimension of sake, down to the objects that accompany it, such as the masu - the small wooden box once used to measure rice and from which sake is drunk during ceremonies or inaugurations. Simple gestures that tell part of Japan’s story.
Sébastien Lemoine’s story is not one of a spectacular career change, but of a transition patiently shaped over the years. That of a man who found in sake a space where culture, technique, and transmission meet. And who, after more than twenty-two years living in Japan, continues to build this bridge between a Japanese tradition and an audience learning to discover it differently.

blocks.section: Itinéraires singuliers podcast - From the trading floor to sake breweries: Sébastien Lemoine’s rediscovered sense of purpose
blocks.text: Leaving a well-established career in international finance to turn to Japanese sake may seem like a radical shift. For Sébastien Lemoine, it is above all the culmination of a quest: finding meaning again. That is the word he chooses to sum up his journey. After years on trading floors, in a demanding environment sometimes dominated by greed and performance, he realizes his energy is gradually fading. The shock of the global financial crisis, followed by the Tohoku disaster in 2011, accelerates his reflection.

blocks.section: Itinéraires singuliers podcast - From the trading floor to sake breweries: Sébastien Lemoine’s rediscovered sense of purpose
blocks.text: Japan is a country he has known for a long time. He first came in 1986 as a student, drawn by the language and the culture. He then returned regularly, eventually settling there for extended periods. He has seen the country evolve, age, and change pace. What was once a very young, vibrant Japan - onsen full of children, overflowing energy in Roppongi - has given way to an older society. Yet his attachment has only grown stronger. He walks, cycles, crosses countryside and cities, and finds in this close relationship with the country a form of obviousness, almost a feeling of being “where he belongs”.

blocks.section: Itinéraires singuliers podcast - From the trading floor to sake breweries: Sébastien Lemoine’s rediscovered sense of purpose
blocks.text: It was from 2008 that he truly discovered Japanese sake. Not generic sake, but carefully crafted bottles rooted in a culture of long-term commitment. Japanese craftsmanship, he says, is not just a profession but a path. One strives for a perfection that is never fully reached, but approached by integrating each year’s experience, variations in climate, rice, and microorganisms. He cites the Kenbishi brewery in Kobe, which claims continuity across centuries and blends each year sakes drawn from a fifty-year stock to maintain a consistent taste profile despite natural changes.

blocks.text: Interview

blocks.text: Itinéraires singuliers podcast - Blanche Loiseau, between heritage and boldness: a French chef in Japan

blocks.section: Itinéraires singuliers podcast - Blanche Loiseau, between heritage and boldness: a French chef in Japan
blocks.text: She could have stayed in Burgundy, at the heart of the Loiseau house, within the comfort of a well-established group.

blocks.section: Itinéraires singuliers podcast - Blanche Loiseau, between heritage and boldness: a French chef in Japan
blocks.text: But Blanche Loiseau chose to explore other avenues. In 2019, she went to Japan to work in a traditional kaiseki restaurant. A highly codified cuisine, devoid of foreigners and women. For a month, no one spoke to her. So she started washing dishes, observed, offered her help, and gradually earned her place. The sous-chef eventually took her under his wing. She emerged from that year with a rare glimpse into a Japan that is usually closed off. Daughter of a three-star chef and heir to a house whose name resonates throughout French gastronomy, she nonetheless describes a simple childhood in the family kitchen in Saulieu. A rabbit liver tartlet as her madeleine de Proust, a rule passed down by her father - never more than three main flavors on a plate - and a strong conviction: excellence can be pursued without brutality.

blocks.section: Itinéraires singuliers podcast - Blanche Loiseau, between heritage and boldness: a French chef in Japan
blocks.text: Today, she divides her time between France and Japan, working for Loiseau de France while overseeing teams and international openings.

blocks.section: Itinéraires singuliers podcast - Blanche Loiseau, between heritage and boldness: a French chef in Japan
blocks.text: This balance of gentleness and firmness also guides her management style. In Besançon, where she opened a restaurant in 2023, her team is mostly female. She sets a clear framework: if a customer crosses the line, she personally shows them the door, and will go as far as accompanying them to the police station if necessary. She wants demanding kitchens that are also safe, where young people - especially women - can work without being subjected to abuse.

blocks.section: Itinéraires singuliers podcast - Blanche Loiseau, between heritage and boldness: a French chef in Japan
blocks.text: When the opportunity to open a restaurant in Tokyo arises in 2024, she accepts fully aware of what lies ahead. She discovers Japan’s inflexible administrative system, where even opening a bank account can take hours because her first names do not fit into predefined boxes. She also learns to work with very rigorous Japanese teams, sometimes lacking flexibility, but with rare reliability: once a gesture is set, it will be followed all year long.

blocks.section: Itinéraires singuliers podcast - Blanche Loiseau, between heritage and boldness: a French chef in Japan
blocks.text: In this context, she seeks a balance between French culture and Japanese codes. She demonstrates, corrects, and cleans the kitchen alongside her teams so they can leave earlier. Gradually, she earns their respect, without forcing it.

blocks.section: Itinéraires singuliers podcast - Blanche Loiseau, between heritage and boldness: a French chef in Japan
blocks.text: In her cuisine, Blanche finds natural bridges between Burgundy and the archipelago: the trilogy of flavors inherited from her father, purity of ingredients, and strict respect for the seasons. She appreciates the accepted imperfection of Japanese plating, inspired by kintsugi, where nothing is strictly identical yet everything makes sense. And when asked which dish to try in Tokyo, she recommends revisited œufs en meurette - before admitting that, for her, the true dish of Japan is ramen, which she could eat every day.

blocks.section: Itinéraires singuliers podcast - Blanche Loiseau, between heritage and boldness: a French chef in Japan
blocks.text: Her journey is that of a chef who carries a prestigious heritage without being confined by it. A French woman forging her own path between Saulieu and Tokyo, between tradition and movement, guided by a constant line: high standards, respect, and a certain idea of kindness in the kitchen.

title: Itinéraires Singuliers Podcast - From Paris to Fukui: the odyssey of Virginie, a creator who brings together art and fashion in Japan
description:
A French artist chooses the provinces over the fashion capitals and, through sheer perseverance, builds a brand that sells directly to Japan’s most discerning customers. Itinéraires Singuliers dedicates this episode to Virginie Lefèvre – founder of the brand Viruxiny – and to what her journey reveals about creative entrepreneurship in Japan.
Born to draw and paint, trained in fine arts and later in fashion, Virginie arrived in Japan 25 years ago to teach at Esmod. One year was supposed to be enough. But a profound aesthetic and human encounter rooted her on the archipelago. Marriage, motherhood, and an unexpected detour through Fukui – a discreet prefecture, yet an industrial giant in knitwear and techno-sozai materials. Where others might have seen a dead end, she saw an opportunity. She opened a small shop, met workshops supplying major luxury houses, learned the language, sales, and even sewing. From scratch.
Her vision of fashion is both simple and radical: to wear art. Each Viruxiny piece carries a positive message – love, protection of the sea and the earth, cultural blending – sometimes with a playful French touch, like a stylized Eiffel Tower. Against fast fashion and ultra fast fashion, she stands for creative honesty, proximity to her clients, and the long game. Little internet, a lot of fieldwork. She favors pop-up stores, listens to feedback, and refines her offer around two complementary axes: accessible pieces that create attachment and more intricate creations for true fashion lovers.
Behind the smiles and politeness, in Japan, business is business. Being a woman and a foreigner comes with its share of doubts and closed doors. So Virginie steps up to the front line. She sells herself, oversees her artistic direction, manages the numbers, speaks Japanese, and sets boundaries. They want her behind the cash register – she takes the cash register. She’s told that “in front of Japanese customers, it would be better to have Japanese staff” – she proves them wrong with results. A key anecdote: a group of artisans entrusted her with a mini collection, considered too risky with a designer not born in Fukui. She took it back and sold it out in a pop-up. More recently in Ginza, she achieved the highest clothing sales figures, outperforming established national brands. Respect earned on the ground.
Why Fukui instead of Tokyo or Paris? Because growing there means learning everything – from operating a sewing machine to drafting quotes, from local sourcing to understanding the codes of department stores. This school of reality built a solid network: loyal clients, department store directors, multiple agents (to stay independent), and allied entrepreneurs. And it shaped a conviction useful to anyone dreaming of setting up in Japan: rules of politeness must be respected, but a touch of kind audacity opens doors. Call, follow up, send a physical dossier when needed, show that you’re ready to work hard – and keep your promises.
On the practical side, the episode demystifies administration in Japan. You can start small as a sole proprietor, test your creations in local markets, handle your own accounting while volumes are modest, and bring in an accountant when things take off. Japanese language skills help, of course, but effort and reliability earn admiration. Japanese customers are demanding when it comes to quality and finishing – “they spot the tiny stitch that’s off” – and that’s a good thing: their standards clarify what excellence means, prevent shortcuts, and push you to do better.
A recent milestone: Nishiginza. In an environment dominated by massive retail operations, a confidential brand posted the top clothing sales. A clear validation of a model built on authenticity, direct sales, and consistency. And the next steps are already taking shape: incorporation as a Kabushiki Kaisha under review, national development through pop-ups, an upscale line leaning toward couture, and eventually, international expansion. Always with the credo that has guided her from day one: forward, ahead.
This episode isn’t just the story of a brand. It’s the roadmap of a creator who proves that you can remain an artist while becoming a business leader in Japan – without losing your voice.If you love stories where art meets commerce, where one learns to sell without selling out, and where a provincial gamble becomes a winning strategy, press play!Discover how Virginie built Viruxiny customer by customer – and what her journey reveals about how today’s creators can access the Japanese market.
https://www.instagram.com/viruxiny

title: Itinéraires Singuliers Podcast - From Pharmacy to Distillation: How François Combes created Nagura, a Premium Rum born in Ishigaki
description:
Itinéraires Singuliers dedicates this episode to François Combes – founder of Nagura – and to what his journey reveals about artisanal entrepreneurship in Japan, in the Okinawa archipelago where agricultural tradition meets innovation.
A trained pharmacist, François arrived in Japan in the 1990s for a product launch. He hadn’t planned to stay. Yet opportunity turned into belonging. His career took him through laboratories, distribution, pharmacy ownership, and finally real estate – always guided by the same instinct: spot the openings, step in, and learn by doing. Real estate eventually led him to Ishigaki, a gem of Okinawa – an agricultural and maritime island devoted to sugarcane, wagyu, and a fiercely protected rural way of life. Where others saw isolation, he saw an opportunity: after Japanese whisky and Japanese gin, why not a Japanese rum rooted in Ishigaki’s terroir?
His method is straightforward and deliberate: start, learn by doing, and solve one problem a day. Find farmland without being a farmer, convince the city hall and the prefecture, secure alcohol and agricultural licenses, import equipment, and prove sanitary compliance piece by piece. Build trust with local growers, listen before speaking, and earn acceptance. Rather than buying an existing operation, he built his own distillery. Two years later came the first production – and an unambiguous verdict: 'It’s good.'
Nagura proudly claims a Japanese identity. Locally selected typhoon-resistant sugarcane, hand-cut to prevent unwanted fermentations, pressed immediately, and distilled by a whisky-trained distiller for precision rather than effect. Nothing goes to waste: leaves and bagasse go back to farmers, vinasse becomes fertilizer. Minimal plastic, no boxes, Japanese labels. A small team of five to six people, including a local unit of workers with disabilities who handle pressing – a tangible way, as François puts it, to 'give back to the island.'
When it comes to the market, François chose a short, dense funnel: first Ishigaki, then Miyako and Okinawa, followed by a few carefully selected addresses in Tokyo, Kyoto, and Osaka. The goal: a premium brand that grows through tasting, distillery visits, and bartender recommendations. The response? Connoisseurs speak of excellence, and the very first batch earned a gold medal in London. The aim isn’t to flood the internet, but to build a strong reputation among bars, hotels, and restaurants capable of telling the story behind the product.
The episode also breaks a few myths. Starting a company in Japan isn’t the hardest part. The real challenges lie with local banks that take their time, administrative licensing processes, and the strict rules of agricultural zoning. The key, according to François, isn’t waving a French business card as a golden ticket, but consistency: speaking Japanese, being on the ground, accepting early slowness, delivering on time, listening to feedback, and striving for operational perfection at every step – from harvesting to barrel aging, whether in bourbon casks, Japanese whisky barrels, or, more rarely, mizunara oak when it makes ecological sense.
The turning point came when Ishigaki’s bars began serving the rum. 'It’s their rum – the island’s rum,' says François. That local recognition changed everything: Nagura was no longer seen as a Frenchman’s project, but as an island’s pride, a product born from its soil and carried by its people. This sense of ownership became both a shield against failure – the island supports it – and a springboard to Tokyo, where authenticity rooted in place sparks curiosity.
What’s next? Strengthening roots in Okinawa, expanding carefully across Japan, and opening export windows once aged stock allows it. Always guided by the same credo: succeed first where you are. The episode becomes a how-to guide for building in Japan outside the megacities: choose a territory, enter humbly into its networks, respect local standards, and keep your product promise.
This isn’t just the story of a spirit. It’s the story of a transfer of know-how – from pharmacy to distillation – and a collective learning process where farmers, workers, bartenders, and visitors shape the brand as much as its founder. If you love stories where quality outweighs volume, where you sell without selling out, and where an island shapes both a flavor and a vision, listen to the episode. Discover how François Combes built Nagura, field by field, glass by glass – and what it reveals about artisanal entrepreneurship in Japan today.

title: Itinéraires Singuliers Podcast - From translator to sports commentator: how Florent Dabadie built his place in Japan
description:
Arriving in Japan in 1994, Florent Dabadie did not plan to work in sports. A literature lover, trained in Oriental languages, he discovered a country whose social framework matched his sensibilities: a highly codified attention to others, politeness viewed as the foundation of living together. Where many see constraint, he sees a structure that reassures and stimulates.
The turning point came almost by chance. Then a young editorial coordinator for Hachette in Tokyo, he responded to a job ad: the Japan Football Association was looking for an interpreter for a French coach. A rare profile, a unique opportunity. He suddenly found himself thrust into the heart of professional football: crowded press conferences, the discipline of the locker room, travels to the four corners of the world. A crash course not only in language, but in observing cultures.
This immersion revealed a paradox to him: on the international stage, Japanese players face a cultural shock as much as a sporting one. Domestic football remains sheltered, perhaps too much so. These athletes therefore need to be prepared for what awaits them beyond the national cocoon: intensity, confrontation, unpredictability.
Moving into sports journalism, first in football then in tennis, Florent observed that sport has become in Japan a vector for openness. The national team captures public attention far more than the domestic league. Organizers take great care in their hospitality, foreign athletes feel confident, journalists find it easier to engage in conversation than elsewhere. Top-level sport has become a showcase for the country to the world.
Yet everyday life does not come down to the hospitality extended to visitors. Integrating the codes takes time: hierarchy, rituals, caution in relationships. One must find room to maneuver without upsetting the balance. Florent speaks of adaptation, not renunciation: learning the rules in order to know when and how to deviate from them.
On the pitch as in the stands, another distinct feature remains: the atmosphere is passionate yet controlled. Supporters are committed, but helpful. Few disturbances. It is a family experience. A notable contrast with the image of football in Europe.
After 25 years in the field, his conclusion is pragmatic: curiosity is a method. It makes it possible to listen, to decode, to build bridges between two cultures that sometimes struggle to understand each other, especially in humor or direct expression. It also helps one remain oneself without becoming isolated.
Florent Dabadie did not choose Japan for its exoticism, but because he feels at ease there. By speaking about sport, he connects two worlds every day that are trying to understand each other better.

title: Itinéraires Singuliers Podcast - In just one year in Tokyo, Gemmyo shines bright: Pauline Laigneau’s lessons on success
description:
Opening a French fine jewelry house in Tokyo could seem like a daunting challenge. For Pauline Laigneau, founder of Gemmyo, it was instead the natural extension of a principle she has followed from the very beginning: independence of mind.
More than a motto, it’s her way of life. Not acting to please, but acting with integrity. This compass led her far from the academic path set by her education at the prestigious École Normale Supérieure. Instead of an intellectual career, she chose entrepreneurship — sparked by an aesthetic revelation before an engagement ring: wearable sculptures, stones millions of years old, symbols meant to be passed on. She saw a magnificent but frozen world, where warmth was missing. Gemmyo was born from the desire to put colored gemstones back at the center, combining precision, sincerity, and accessibility.
Why Tokyo rather than elsewhere in Asia? Because, according to Pauline, Japanese clients share the same taste as Parisians: discretion, refinement, and meaning. No loud logos — just “intentional jewelry.” Japan became a bold, intuitive move, without endless market studies. Omotesando felt like the natural twin of Saint-Germain-des-Prés: broad streets, art galleries, quiet elegance. The boutique brings Parisian codes (herringbone parquet floors) into subtle dialogue with local ones (stone ceilings, sliding screens for privacy). The construction even finished ahead of schedule — a rarity — and from day one, customers understood the balance: French spirit, Japanese precision.
A clear lesson soon emerged: what works in France works in Japan. Each time the team over-adapted, it backfired — smaller ring sizes, the wrong inventory, flashy influencer campaigns that didn’t resonate. The turnaround came by returning to Gemmyo’s fundamentals: intimate events with real clients, honest storytelling, made-to-order craftsmanship in France, and personal meaning expressed through each gemstone. In the showroom, they don’t sell objects; they adjust symbols.
The Tokyo team of three Japanese advisors — led by Erika-san — maintains a daily link with Paris through WhatsApp and Slack, even joining company seminars in France. Service follows Japanese etiquette, but adds a distinctly Gemmyo touch: genuine advice, even the courage to say no when a piece doesn’t suit. That frankness, rare in Japan, builds trust. And while Japanese preparation is meticulous to the extreme, management strives to focus that precision on what truly matters.
The results speak for themselves. In its first year, the Tokyo boutique generated around €2 million in sales, with the feeling that growth is just beginning. The market confirmed the intuition: many clients were looking for an authentic French maison, rooted in France but open to the world without arrogance. In the boutique, stories multiply — a sapphire chosen for the color of one’s eyes, a tourmaline tied to a memory, a cognac diamond marking a life moment. Each piece carries intention and emotion.
Next steps point toward Kansai. A two-weekend pop-up at Kyoto’s Hotel Okura booked out in 24 hours — 66 appointments — clear proof of demand. Kyoto now appears as the natural next location, perhaps followed by Fukuoka or Nagoya. Expansion at Gemmyo doesn’t mean spreading wide, but growing precisely — excelling locally, then expanding when the community itself asks for it.
Ultimately, Gemmyo’s story in Japan is less about cultural contrast than mutual resonance. Japan values mastery, preparation, and beauty. Gemmyo brings warmth, authenticity, and human connection. Between the two emerges a shared language — that of meaningful craftsmanship. Staying true to oneself here isn’t rigidity. It’s a method. And sometimes, the best way to adapt to Japan is not to over-adapt.
Website: https://www.gemmyo.com/ja/

title: Itinéraires singuliers – Yuji Hirayama :World climbing champion looks back on his journey, his passion for climbing and his strong connection with France
description:
He could have continued his journey in Japan. Yet at 19, Yuji Hirayama set off for France with one goal in mind: to discover how Europe’s best climbers trained and to reach the very highest level of the sport himself.
This experience would profoundly transform not only his approach to climbing, but also his outlook on the world. After spending several years in France, he returned to Japan and became one of the most iconic climbers of his generation. More than 40 years after he first started climbing, he continues to pursue the sport while sharing his experience through his climbing gyms and various projects dedicated to the discipline.
“The environment is important. I wanted to go to Europe to learn how to climb at the highest level and bring that experience back to Japan.”
Setting Off for France
Yuji Hirayama discovered climbing at the age of 15 and quickly set himself the goal of competing with the best climbers in the world. After his first trip to the United States at 17, he became particularly interested in the European climbing scene and the training methods he encountered, notably through French climbing magazines.
At 19, he decided to move to France with several friends. After arriving in Marseille, he settled in the Luberon region. He spoke very little French and found himself in a country whose customs and culture were still largely unfamiliar to him.
Beyond climbing, the experience quickly became a genuine cultural immersion. He learned the language, discovered a different way of life and became familiar with another approach to sport. He was particularly struck by the more structured preparation of French climbers, for whom training and recovery each played an important role.
Above all, this period allowed him to take a step back and reassess his own climbing. Balancing the discipline of European training with a certain freedom in the way he approached the sport, Yuji Hirayama gradually developed his own philosophy of climbing.
From the Summit to Years of Doubt
The results soon followed. Hirayama reached the highest levels of international climbing and took on some of the hardest routes of his time. Yet behind his performances, a more personal question gradually emerged: why keep climbing once the goals he had set himself as a teenager had been achieved?
For several years, training and competition became a routine. The pursuit of performance no longer always provided a sense of purpose.
Another trip to the United States, at the age of 25, marked a turning point. His perspective on the world began to change. He started looking at the shapes, materials and objects around him with a newfound curiosity. He came to understand that all those years devoted to climbing had also shaped the way he thought and perceived his surroundings.
“Not giving up really mattered. Even when you can’t immediately find the answer, you can keep moving forward and take the time to look for it.”
This realisation gradually helped him rediscover a more peaceful relationship with climbing. It was no longer just about results, but also a way to explore, learn and continue to grow.
Sharing Climbing Beyond Competition
After dedicating much of his life to competition and elite-level climbing, Yuji Hirayama also decided to create spaces where others could discover and practise the sport.
He founded Base Camp, a network of climbing gyms primarily located in the Tokyo and Saitama regions. What was initially intended as a personal training space gradually became a place open to a wide range of people: children, elite athletes and older climbers simply looking to stay active and healthy.
Today, his commitment extends beyond the climbing gyms themselves. Based in a region close to the mountains of Saitama, he also takes part in projects aimed at revitalising local communities through climbing, promoting natural climbing areas and building connections between climbers, visitors and residents.
His journey between France and Japan naturally informs this desire to build bridges. Having spent several years in Europe, he explains that he also came to rediscover his own country and certain aspects of his Japanese identity.
Today, Yuji Hirayama continues to climb, but his ambitions extend far beyond performance. He hopes to see Japanese climbing continue to grow and embrace a wider range of approaches, particularly outdoor climbing.
After more than 40 years in the sport, he continues to move forward with the same curiosity he had when he first started: discovering new routes, new places and new ways of practising a discipline that, for him, has always been a way of exploring the world.

More than 40 years after he first started climbing, he continues to pursue the sport while sharing his experience through his climbing gyms and various projects dedicated to the discipline.

blocks.section: Itinéraires singuliers – Yuji Hirayama :World climbing champion looks back on his journey, his passion for climbing and his strong connection with France
blocks.text: “The environment is important. I wanted to go to Europe to learn how to climb at the highest level and bring that experience back to Japan.”

blocks.section: Setting Off for France
blocks.text: Setting Off for France

blocks.section: Setting Off for France
blocks.text: Yuji Hirayama discovered climbing at the age of 15 and quickly set himself the goal of competing with the best climbers in the world. After his first trip to the United States at 17, he became particularly interested in the European climbing scene and the training methods he encountered, notably through French climbing magazines.

blocks.section: Setting Off for France
blocks.text: At 19, he decided to move to France with several friends. After arriving in Marseille, he settled in the Luberon region. He spoke very little French and found himself in a country whose customs and culture were still largely unfamiliar to him.

blocks.section: Setting Off for France
blocks.text: Beyond climbing, the experience quickly became a genuine cultural immersion. He learned the language, discovered a different way of life and became familiar with another approach to sport. He was particularly struck by the more structured preparation of French climbers, for whom training and recovery each played an important role.

blocks.section: Setting Off for France
blocks.text: Above all, this period allowed him to take a step back and reassess his own climbing. Balancing the discipline of European training with a certain freedom in the way he approached the sport, Yuji Hirayama gradually developed his own philosophy of climbing.

blocks.section: From the Summit to Years of Doubt
blocks.text: From the Summit to Years of Doubt

blocks.section: From the Summit to Years of Doubt
blocks.text: The results soon followed. Hirayama reached the highest levels of international climbing and took on some of the hardest routes of his time. Yet behind his performances, a more personal question gradually emerged: why keep climbing once the goals he had set himself as a teenager had been achieved?

blocks.section: From the Summit to Years of Doubt
blocks.text: For several years, training and competition became a routine. The pursuit of performance no longer always provided a sense of purpose.

blocks.section: From the Summit to Years of Doubt
blocks.text: Another trip to the United States, at the age of 25, marked a turning point. His perspective on the world began to change. He started looking at the shapes, materials and objects around him with a newfound curiosity. He came to understand that all those years devoted to climbing had also shaped the way he thought and perceived his surroundings.

blocks.section: From the Summit to Years of Doubt
blocks.text: “Not giving up really mattered. Even when you can’t immediately find the answer, you can keep moving forward and take the time to look for it.”

blocks.section: From the Summit to Years of Doubt
blocks.text: This realisation gradually helped him rediscover a more peaceful relationship with climbing. It was no longer just about results, but also a way to explore, learn and continue to grow.

blocks.section: Sharing Climbing Beyond Competition
blocks.text: Sharing Climbing Beyond Competition

blocks.section: Sharing Climbing Beyond Competition
blocks.text: After dedicating much of his life to competition and elite-level climbing, Yuji Hirayama also decided to create spaces where others could discover and practise the sport.

blocks.section: Sharing Climbing Beyond Competition
blocks.text: He founded Base Camp, a network of climbing gyms primarily located in the Tokyo and Saitama regions. What was initially intended as a personal training space gradually became a place open to a wide range of people: children, elite athletes and older climbers simply looking to stay active and healthy.

blocks.section: Sharing Climbing Beyond Competition
blocks.text: Today, his commitment extends beyond the climbing gyms themselves. Based in a region close to the mountains of Saitama, he also takes part in projects aimed at revitalising local communities through climbing, promoting natural climbing areas and building connections between climbers, visitors and residents.

blocks.section: Sharing Climbing Beyond Competition
blocks.text: His journey between France and Japan naturally informs this desire to build bridges. Having spent several years in Europe, he explains that he also came to rediscover his own country and certain aspects of his Japanese identity.

blocks.section: Sharing Climbing Beyond Competition
blocks.text: Today, Yuji Hirayama continues to climb, but his ambitions extend far beyond performance. He hopes to see Japanese climbing continue to grow and embrace a wider range of approaches, particularly outdoor climbing.

blocks.section: Sharing Climbing Beyond Competition
blocks.text: After more than 40 years in the sport, he continues to move forward with the same curiosity he had when he first started: discovering new routes, new places and new ways of practising a discipline that, for him, has always been a way of exploring the world.

blocks.text: Japan ends its negative interest-rate policy

blocks.section: Japan ends its negative interest-rate policy
blocks.text: This week, Japan’s central bank raised interest rates for the first time in 17 years. Still, rates are remaining close to zero, opening a symbolic bre

blocks.section: Japan ends its negative interest-rate policy
blocks.text: After years of deflation with little change in prices, wages and cost of money, Japanese people are assessing how to adapt to higher borrowing costs.

blocks.section: Japan ends its negative interest-rate policy
blocks.text: Between them, the way small business owners will cope will have far-reaching implications, in an economy where small and medium-sized businesses employ some 70% of the workforce, and where private consumption accounts for more than half of gross domestic product .

blocks.section: Japan ends its negative interest-rate policy
blocks.text: Japanese companies and households have been content to play the deflationary game , hoarding cash and cutting costs. As a result, the economy found itself in a deflationary vicious circle, with stagnating growth and wages. It may prove difficult to shake off this deflationary mindset, given that large companies have been granting substantial wage increases for decades.

blocks.section: Japan ends its negative interest-rate policy
blocks.text: According to a Reuters survey conducted on Thursday, some 60% of Japanese companies expect interest rates to reach 0.25% by the end of the year . As a result, many said they were looking to anticipate spending before borrowing costs rise.

title: Japan Experience joins the Havas Voyages Group and accelerates its growth
description:
Japan Experience announced in late December 2025 that it had been acquired 100 percent by the Havas Voyages group (Marietton Développement), the leading tourism player in France.
Japan Experience, a leading player in travel to Japan
Founded in 1981, Japan Experience has established itself over the years as a reference player for travel to Japan, with a unique positioning covering the entire value chain - travel agency, tour operator, and destination management company. The company employed nearly 100 staff across Europe (Paris, Milan, Madrid, Berlin, London) and Japan (Tokyo, Kyoto). Each year, around 300,000 travelers benefited from its services. In 2025, the company generated revenue of 70 million euros and had been profitable continuously since its creation.
This partnership with Havas Voyages formed part of a strategy focused on growth and complementarity. The Marietton Développement group aimed to strengthen its expertise in Japan, a rapidly expanding destination, while leveraging Japan Experience’s well-recognized digital know-how. In 2024, Japan welcomed 37 million international visitors, including 400,000 French travelers, and the Japanese authorities were targeting 60 million foreign visitors by 2030.
The transaction enabled Japan Experience to rely on Havas Voyages’ international network and distribution strength, while maintaining its specialist positioning and digital DNA. The stated objective was to double the size of the company within five years, particularly through international expansion and B2B development.
“Joining Havas Voyages means offering Japan Experience a strong and visionary partner to accelerate our development, while preserving what makes us strong - our passion for Japan, the expertise of our teams, and digital innovation in the service of our clients,” said Thierry Maincent, CEO of Japan Experience.
Following the transaction, Japan Experience’s governance remained unchanged. Thierry Maincent retained his role as CEO and joined the executive committee of the Havas Voyages group to support this new phase of development.
Irasshai: a concept store dedicated to Japanese culinary culture in Paris
Alongside his activities in tourism, Thierry Maincent co-founded the Irasshai concept store in Paris in 2023 with Xavier Marchand. Located in the heart of the French capital and spanning 800 square meters, Irasshai brings together a grocery store offering products sourced directly from Japan, a tea room that turns into a sake bar in the evening, a gastronomic restaurant, and a shokudo, a Japanese-style canteen.
The venue also hosts collaborations with Japanese institutions and brands.

title: Japan honoured as Country of the Year at 8th edition of Viva Technology
description:
At the upcoming 8th edition of Viva Technology, Japan will be celebrated as Country of the Year, consolidating its position as a leading partner of Europe's largest startup and technology event, which takes place in Paris from 22 to 25 May.
Renowned for its track record of disruptive innovations, Japan has firmly established itself as a global technology powerhouse. This acknowledgment underscores Japan's unwavering commitment to pushing technological boundaries and creating an environment conducive to pioneering advancements.
At the core of Japan's forward-looking vision is "Society 5.0," a paradigm shift aimed at addressing and surmounting societal challenges by seamlessly integrating innovations, including AI, across industries and daily life, ultimately enhancing people's lives with comfort and sustainability. Japan's prominent presence at Viva Technology will showcase an inspiring ecosystem of startups offering visionary solutions for the future. In recent years, the Japanese government has passionately worked towards positioning Japan as one of the world's most startup-friendly nations, with a ambitious goal of increasing the number of unicorns and new business launches in the Japanese capital tenfold over five years.
“We are thrilled to collaborate and forge strong connections with Japan for this edition of Viva Technology. In light of Japan’s rich history as a pioneer of tech and innovation, we are proud to promote the Japanese startup dynamic. This flourishing ecosystem is eminently represented by companies from a wide range of sectors, and VivaTech is excited to bring their contributions to the rest of the world.”, said Co-Presidents of Viva Technology, Maurice Lévy and Pierre Louette, along with Managing Director François Bitouzet.
As a catalyst for innovation and transformation, VivaTech is providing Japanese startups with a unique opportunity to join a global community, foster business relationships through networking and investor meetings, promote their ventures, and actively engage in the VivaTech conference program.
Beyond economic implications, this strategic partnership reaffirms Japan's robust diplomatic ties with France and Europe, underscoring VivaTech's role as the epicenter of international tech.

title: Japan is struggling to break out of its deflationary cycle
description: While consumer prices rose by 2.8% in February, Japan is struggling to break out of its deflationary cycle.

blocks.text: Foresight

blocks.section: Japan is struggling to break out of its deflationary cycle
blocks.text: Japan is struggling to break out of its deflationary cycle

blocks.section: Japan is struggling to break out of its deflationary cycle
blocks.text: While consumer prices rose by 2.8% in February, Japan is struggling to break out of its deflationary cycle.

blocks.section: Japan is struggling to break out of its deflationary cycle
blocks.text: On February 22, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications announced that the consumer price index (2020 = 100) for February stood at 106.5, up 2.8% on the same period last year. At the same time, Japan experienced its first expansion in four months, with growth 0.8 points higher than in January.

blocks.section: Japan is struggling to break out of its deflationary cycle
blocks.text: The Bank of Japan has opted for large-scale monetary easing on the grounds that the goal of 2% price inflation is in sight, but the government has not yet declared the end of deflation.

title: Japan Post continues acquisition of Aflac
description: Japan Post continues to acquire shares in insurance giant Aflac.

blocks.text: Foresight

blocks.section: Japan Post continues acquisition of Aflac
blocks.text: Japan Post continues acquisition of Aflac

blocks.section: Japan Post continues acquisition of Aflac
blocks.text: Japan Post continues to acquire shares in insurance giant Aflac.

blocks.section: Japan Post continues acquisition of Aflac
blocks.text: Japan Post continues its acquisition of insurance giant Aflac . The business alliance began in 2018, with the latter deciding to acquire Aflac shares at a cost of around 270 billion yen.

blocks.section: Japan Post continues acquisition of Aflac
blocks.text: It had already acquired around 7% of Aflac shares by 2020, and is set to continue increasing its stake in the company.

blocks.section: Japan Post continues acquisition of Aflac
blocks.text: By holding shares today for more than four years, it should increase its voting rights to around 20%. The exercise of the right is expected to be approved at Aflac’s Annual General Meeting on May 6.

blocks.section: Japan Post continues acquisition of Aflac
blocks.text: The acquisition is expected to bolster the business of Japan Post, which is experiencing a decline in postal demand due to the spread of digitalization. The group’s sales target for fiscal 2023 was 91.9 billion yen.

title: Japan Shines as Country of the Year at VivaTech 2024 !
description:
From May 22 to 25, Paris was abuzz with innovation and inspiration at VivaTechnology, Europe's premier start-up and tech event. This year, Japan proudly took center stage, being honored as the Country of the Year for 2024.
In collaboration with the CCI Paris Ile-de-France and CCI Hauts-de-France, the CCI France Japon orchestrated B2B meetings program. This initiative allowed eight Japanese start-ups to connect and collaborate with their French counterparts, fostering exciting new partnerships and innovations.
On the eve of the show, the 21st of May, the ‘Japan Official Ecosystem Meet Up Night’ was held at the Japanese Ambassador's Residence. This prestigious event, built in collaboration with METI, JETRO, and the Tokyo Metropolitan Government, set the stage for meaningful exchanges and future collaborations.
In the event, ecosystem players in Tokyo showcased TIB (Tokyo Innovation Base), which acts as a global node of innovation where diverse individuals connect and support innovators. Additionally, they introduced SusHi Tech Tokyo (Sustainable High City Tech Tokyo), a tech event that aims to develop technology to tackle various urban challenges.
Stay tuned as Japan continues to lead the way in technological advancements and innovative solutions !
Thank you again for being such an amazing partner to work with. The CCI France Japon is excited to work together in the future.

title: Japanese cybersecurity recruitment on the rise
description: Facing the threat of cyber-attacks, more and more Japanese companies are recruiting in the field of cybersecurity.

blocks.text: Foresight

blocks.section: Japanese cybersecurity recruitment on the rise
blocks.text: Japanese cybersecurity recruitment on the rise

blocks.section: Japanese cybersecurity recruitment on the rise
blocks.text: Facing the threat of cyber-attacks, more and more Japanese companies are recruiting in the field of cybersecurity.

blocks.section: Japanese cybersecurity recruitment on the rise
blocks.text: A “ red ocean in a red ocean ”, according to Recruit (a Japanese company specializing in human resources). Competition for cybersecurity talent is fierce in Japan. According to a Recruit study published this month, the number of cybersecurity-related jobs was 24.3 times higher in 2023 than in 2002.

blocks.section: Japanese cybersecurity recruitment on the rise
blocks.text: The years 2018 - 2019 saw a particular increase linked to the growing concern about cyber attack risks during the Tokyo Olympics, which were due to take place in 2020.

blocks.section: Japanese cybersecurity recruitment on the rise
blocks.text: The rise in demand for jobs since 2020 can be explained by the pandemic. A number of cyber-attacks have targeted the shift to teleworking, leaving corporate VPNs vulnerable. Faced with such risks, some companies have been forced to suspend operations.

blocks.section: Japanese cybersecurity recruitment on the rise
blocks.text: Although the number of opportunities is increasing, few people have actually changed jobs. Recruit states “[that] it is difficult to recruit people with immediate skills, unless you can offer them attractive annual salaries in line with market conditions.”

blocks.section: Japanese cybersecurity recruitment on the rise
blocks.text: Faced with this recruitment difficulty, companies are forced to review their recruitment strategy, in particular by offering in-house training courses. In some cases, companies are calling on IT specialists even if they have no practical experience in cybersecurity.

description: The Ministry of Economy recently promised to fund the development of supercomputers to help five companies working in the AI sector.

blocks.section: Japanese government grants over 70 billion yen in AI subsidies
blocks.text: Japanese government grants over 70 billion yen in AI subsidies

blocks.section: Japanese government grants over 70 billion yen in AI subsidies
blocks.text: The Ministry of Economy recently promised to fund the development of supercomputers to help five companies working in the AI sector.

blocks.section: Japanese government grants over 70 billion yen in AI subsidies
blocks.text: Generative AI (artificial intelligence) is developing rapidly, and needs are growing in every country.

blocks.section: Japanese government grants over 70 billion yen in AI subsidies
blocks.text: However, its growth requires “supercomputers” capable of processing information rapidly. In Japan, there is little national infrastructure in place, with AI development dependent on large American companies .

blocks.section: Japanese government grants over 70 billion yen in AI subsidies
blocks.text: Against this backdrop, Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) recently pledged to subsidize five companies to the tune of 72.5 billion yen to boost AI development .

blocks.section: Japanese government grants over 70 billion yen in AI subsidies
blocks.text: According to officials, this decision is part of a drive to develop supercomputers by local companies, but also to ensure the country's economic security.

blocks.text: Details will be announced shortly.

title: Japanese land prices rise for the third year running
description: Land prices in Japan have risen by 3% for the first time since the speculative bubble.

blocks.text: Foresight

blocks.section: Japanese land prices rise for the third year running
blocks.text: Japanese land prices rise for the third year running

blocks.section: Japanese land prices rise for the third year running
blocks.text: Land prices in Japan have risen by 3% for the first time since the speculative bubble.

blocks.section: Japanese land prices rise for the third year running
blocks.text: Announced on March 26 by the Ministry of Land and Transport (Kokudo-kotsu-sho), Japanese land prices rose by 2.4% year-on-year . This is the third consecutive year of increases, and the highest rate of growth since the speculative bubble.

blocks.section: Japanese land prices rise for the third year running
blocks.text: Indeed, after the bubble burst, land prices in Japan remained negative for a long time. However, the rise in land prices marks a turning point in Japan’s deflationary recovery, going hand in hand with rising equities and wages. The question is whether this momentum can be maintained in the future, while stimulating the economy at the same time.

blocks.section: Japanese land prices rise for the third year running
blocks.text: In addition to strong housing demand in the main metropolitan areas (Tokyo, Osaka and Nagoya) and the four regional cities (Sapporo, Sendai, Hiroshima and Fukuoka), rural areas are also affected .

blocks.section: Japanese land prices rise for the third year running
blocks.text: In Tokyo, the return of office work has led to a reduction in telecommuting, with commercial land rising by an average of 7.0%. According to Mitsubishi UFJ Trust and Banking Corporation, vacancy rates around JR Yamanote stations remain at around 3%.

blocks.section: Japanese land prices rise for the third year running
blocks.text: For the eighteenth year running, the highest price was 55.7 million yen (approximately $370,000) per square meter in Ginza, Tokyo.

blocks.section: Japan's Tourist Industry: Change in the Last 10 Years and What’s Beyond
blocks.text: Over the past decade, Japan's tourism industry has shifted from a domestic orientation to an international tourist orientation . This shift has been evident in various ways, such as the significant increase in inbound tourists, which has propelled Japanese department store sales to record highs. Additionally, hotel operators have responded to this shift by planning to open properties designed to attract these tourists at new destinations.

blocks.section: Japan's Tourist Industry: Change in the Last 10 Years and What’s Beyond
blocks.text: The shift in Japan's tourism industry is not just a change in one sector, but a transformation that could have far-reaching effects across industries. This event will delve into how the shift unlocked untapped markets in Japan, presenting a unique chance for growth and development .
